opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's important to be careful here, because there's a temptation to hear "the intentional stance" and conclude that it's merely subjective, that it's just a matter of taste whether we describe something as having beliefs and desires. That's not really how Dennett meant it, and it's not how I'd put it either.

When we adopt the intentional stance towards something, whether it's a person, a chess-playing computer, or a large language model, we're treating it as a rational agent with beliefs, desires and goals, and using that to predict and explain its behaviour. Whether the stance is warranted isn't arbitrary. It depends on whether it actually works, whether it gives us predictive and explanatory purchase that we couldn't easily get otherwise. If I try to take the intentional stance towards a thermostat, I can do it, but it buys me very little. With a chess program it buys me a great deal. So there's an objective fact about how useful the stance is, even though the stance is something we take.

So I'd call it perspectival rather than subjective. There's a perspective involved, a way of looking, but it's answerable to the world. And I think that's a Wittgensteinian point as well. Our talk of beliefs and intentions is embedded in shared practices, in a form of life, and the criteria for applying those words are public. They're not private inner judgements.

Where it gets interesting with large language models is that the stance works very well in some respects and breaks down in others. You can usefully say the model "knows" that Paris is the capital of France, but then it'll do something that no creature with genuine beliefs would do, and the stance wobbles. That's why I've emphasised the idea of role play. Rather than saying the model itself has beliefs, it's often more accurate to say it's playing a character, or a superposition of characters, and we can take the intentional stance towards the character being played. That keeps us honest about what's going on without collapsing into either naive anthropomorphism or flat dismissal.

So, in short, I'd resist calling it subjective in the pejorative sense. It's a stance, but stances can be more or less apt, and that aptness is something we can argue about and investigate.

r001.rationale: It describes the stance as treating an entity as having beliefs, desires, and goals to predict and explain its behavior, which communicates using intentional vocabulary to describe it.

r002.rationale: It calls the stance perspectival rather than subjective and says its aptness is answerable to the world.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think we have to be careful about what we mean by "subjectivity" here. Dennett's notion of the intentional stance is that when we treat a system as if it has beliefs and desires and goals, and we predict its behaviour on that basis, we're adopting a particular predictive strategy. And the question is whether adopting that strategy is somehow a matter of mere opinion, a sort of projection on our part that tells us nothing about the system itself.

I don't think that follows at all. Dennett's own view is that the intentional stance is successful in some cases and not in others, and that success or failure is an objective matter. If I take the intentional stance towards a thermostat, I gain very little. I can say it "wants" the room to be twenty degrees, but the physical stance or the design stance does just as well. Whereas if I take the intentional stance towards a chess-playing program, or towards another person, I gain enormous predictive leverage that I simply couldn't get any other way. That difference isn't up to me. It's a fact about the system and about the patterns it exhibits. Dennett has this lovely phrase, "real patterns," and his point is that these patterns are genuinely there in the behaviour, to be discovered rather than invented.

So there's a sense in which there's a perspectival element, yes. You have to adopt a stance, and the stance is something an observer does. But I'd resist the slide from "perspectival" to "subjective" in the pejorative sense of arbitrary or merely a matter of taste. Lots of perfectly objective concepts are perspectival in that way. Whether something counts as a tool, or whether a pattern in the stock market is a trend, depends on there being someone for whom it's a tool or a trend, and yet we can still be right or wrong about it.

Where this gets interesting for me, and where I think the subjectivity worry has more bite, is with large language models. Because here we have systems where the intentional stance is enormously tempting, almost irresistible, since they're trained on human language and produce human-like text. And the question is whether the predictive payoff is really there, or whether we're being seduced by surface features. I think the honest answer is that it's partly there and partly not. Talking about what the model "believes" or "knows" can be a useful shorthand up to a point, but the patterns underneath are quite alien, and the stance can break down in ways it wouldn't for a human. So I'd say the challenge isn't that the intentional stance is subjective. It's that we need to be disciplined and empirical about where it earns its keep and where it leads us astray.

r001.rationale: It describes treating a system as having beliefs, desires, and goals to predict its behavior, which communicates using intentional vocabulary to describe the system.

r002.rationale: It rejects the inference from taking a perspective to subjectivity, calling the intentional stance objective in its success or failure and saying the challenge is not that it is subjective.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think we have to be a little careful about what we mean by subjectivity here. Taking the intentional stance means treating something as having beliefs and desires, and using those to make sense of what it does. That’s a stance we adopt as observers. But it doesn’t follow that we’re attributing subjective experience to the thing we’re interpreting.

You might say a chess program wants to protect its queen, or believes it has a winning position. That can be a useful way of describing its behaviour without suggesting there’s anything it feels like to be that program.

So I’d distinguish the observer’s perspective from the subjectivity of the system itself. And even though the intentional stance is a perspective we bring, it isn’t simply arbitrary: some attributions do a much better job of explaining and predicting behaviour than others.

r001.rationale: It describes treating an entity as having beliefs and desires to make sense of its behavior, which communicates using that vocabulary to describe behavior.

r002.rationale: It says attributing beliefs and desires does not imply subjective experience in the entity being interpreted.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think we need to distinguish two senses of subjectivity here. Taking the intentional stance means treating something as having beliefs and desires in order to make sense of its behaviour. That involves adopting a particular perspective, but it doesn’t necessarily mean that what you say is arbitrary, or just a matter of personal opinion. There can be very good reasons for adopting that perspective: it might allow you to predict what the system will do.

And that’s a separate question from whether the system has a subjective point of view of its own. When I say that a chess program wants to protect its queen, that can be a useful description without implying that there’s anything it feels like to be that program. So I’d be careful about moving from the usefulness of intentional language to a claim about subjective experience.

r001.rationale: It describes treating an entity as having beliefs and desires to make sense of its behavior, and calls this a useful description using intentional language.

r002.rationale: It separates using intentional language from the entity having a subjective point of view or subjective experience.
